Detective Fiction. A literary genre centered on the investigation and solving of a crime, typically murder, through logical deduction, forensic observation, and procedural inquiry. A protagonist—professional detective or amateur investigator—gathers clues, interviews suspects, and ultimately unveils the criminal through reasoning and ingenuity. Originating in the eighteen forties with Edgar Allan Poe, systematized by Arthur Conan Doyle and his Sherlock Holmes stories, and perfected in the nineteen twenties through nineteen thirties by writers like Agatha Christie and Raymond Chandler, detective fiction became one of the most popular and enduring literary forms of the twentieth century. It embodies the modernist faith in logic and the Enlightenment dream that reason can penetrate mystery. Edgar Allan Poe's The Murders in the Rue Morgue, published in eighteen forty-one, is the foundational text; it features C. Auguste Dupin, the first literary detective, who solves a seemingly impossible crime through observation and deduction. Arthur Conan Doyle created Sherlock Holmes from eighteen eighty-seven onward; the Holmes stories became a phenomenon, establishing the archetype of the brilliant, eccentric detective and the bumbling, admiring sidekick, Watson. The Golden Age of detective fiction, spanning the nineteen twenties through nineteen thirties, saw rigid conventions emerge: the locked-room mystery, the fair-play puzzle, and the clue-based solution where readers have access to all evidence needed to solve the crime. Key subgenres include puzzle mysteries—mathematical, logic-based games between author and reader, with Agatha Christie as the supreme master—and hard-boiled detective fiction, an American variant with cynical, morally ambiguous protagonists navigating a corrupt world. Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe and Dashiell Hammett's Sam Spade define the hard-boiled type. Formal properties central to detective fiction include the detective as hero, whose intellectual superiority outpaces ordinary police and laypeople; fair play, where all clues necessary to solve the crime are presented to the reader; closure and order, as the criminal is identified and captured and chaos resolves to rational explanation; and economy of motivation—finite, knowable motives like money, passion, revenge, or hidden identity. Detective fiction embodies Enlightenment rationality: the belief that logic can solve any puzzle and that truth can be recovered through systematic investigation. It remains the world's most widely read literary form and one of the oldest popular genres.
